summary: The hit ratio is 0.8, so the average access time is 0.8 × 75 + 0.2 × 1500 = 360 ns.
steps: The miss ratio is 0.2. Therefore the hit ratio is 1 − 0.2 = 0.8.
A hit takes 75 ns; the main-memory path takes 1500 ns. The question explicitly says that 1500 ns already includes checking the cache.
Weight the complete paths by their probabilities: 0.8 × 75 ns + 0.2 × 1500 ns = 60 ns + 300 ns = 360 ns.
Option a (315 ns) does not match these timings. Options c and d put too much weight on the slow path. The given 0.2 is the miss ratio, not the hit ratio.
takeaway: Read what the miss time includes. Do not add the cache-check time a second time.
imageDescription: Cache memory takes 75 ns; main memory takes 1500 ns including the cache check. The miss ratio is 0.2. Find the approximate average access time.

summary: Equating the two weighted access times gives a cache hit ratio of 5/6, approximately 0.83.
steps: Let h be the shared hit ratio. Under the weighted-path model, system A takes 14h + 80(1 − h) ns. System B takes 12h + 90(1 − h) ns.
The effective times are equal: 80 − 66h = 90 − 78h. Rearranging gives 12h = 10, so h = 10/12 = 5/6 ≈ 0.83.
Check: system A takes 14 × 5/6 + 80 × 1/6 = 25 ns. System B takes 12 × 5/6 + 90 × 1/6 = 25 ns.
Option a, 0.17, approximates the miss ratio 1 − h. Option b does not make the effective times equal; at h = 1 (option d), the times would be 14 ns and 12 ns.
takeaway: Write a separate weighted average for each system, then equate them. The answer requested is the hit ratio.
imageDescription: System A: cache 14 ns, main memory 80 ns. System B: cache 12 ns, main memory 90 ns. Both have the same effective access time and hit ratio. Find the approximate hit ratio.

summary: A cache miss means the requested data is not in the cache. In this question's cache/main-memory model, the CPU fetches it from main memory.
steps: A cache hit means the requested data is available in the cache, so it can be served there. Fetching it from ROM or main memory is not the defining action of a hit.
A cache miss means the requested data is absent from the cache. It cannot be supplied by that cache, which rules out option c.
The CPU must obtain the missing data from the next level of the memory hierarchy, main memory in this question. That is option d. Real processors can have additional cache levels before RAM.
takeaway: Hit: data found in the cache. Miss: continue to the next level of the memory hierarchy.

optionText.a: On a cache hit, fetch data from ROM.
optionText.b: On a cache hit, fetch data from main memory.
optionText.c: On a cache miss, fetch data from cache memory.
optionText.d: On a cache miss, fetch data from main memory.

imageDescription: Choose the appropriate CPU operation associated with cache memory. The four choices pair a cache hit or miss with fetching from ROM, cache or main memory.

summary: The hexadecimal integer part is 291 and the fractional part is one quarter.
steps: Expand each position in base 16: 1×16² + 2×16¹ + 3×16⁰ + 4×16⁻¹.
The integer part is 256 + 32 + 3 = 291. The fractional digit contributes 4/16 = 0.25.
Combine the two parts: 291 + 0.25 = 291.25, option C. A hexadecimal fractional digit has weight 1/16, not 1/8 or 1/10.
takeaway: Positions right of the radix point have negative powers of the base.
imageDescription: Convert hexadecimal 123.4 to decimal. The four numerical choices are listed below.

summary: Both the integer part and the fractional part must be converted.
steps: 23 = 16 + 4 + 2 + 1, so the integer bits are 10111.
0.375 = 3/8 = 1/4 + 1/8, so its binary fraction is .011.
Together they give 10111.011, option A. The .110 alternatives mean 0.75; 11101 means 29 rather than 23.
takeaway: Convert the two sides of the radix point separately.
imageDescription: Choose the binary representation of decimal 23.375. Each choice combines an integer part with a three-bit fraction.

summary: Each octal digit is weighted by a power of eight.
steps: Calculate 512 + 128 + 24 + 4 = 668 for the integer part.
The fractional part is 2/8 = 0.25. The total is 668.25, option B.
takeaway: Do not treat the fractional digit of an octal number as a decimal tenth.
imageDescription: Convert octal 1234.2 into decimal. Four numerical choices follow.

summary: The normal single-precision bit pattern represents positive 14.
steps: Split the bits as 0 | 10000010 | 11000000000000000000000: sign S=0, exponent E=130 and fraction F=1/2+1/4=0.75.
Remove the exponent bias: E−127 = 3. Include the implicit leading 1, giving significand 1+F=1.75.
Evaluate (+1)×2³×1.75 = 14.0, option D. Reading only the stored fraction would give 8×0.75=6.0, the misconception behind option C.
takeaway: A normal IEEE 754 value includes an unstored leading 1.
imageDescription: IEEE 754 binary32 uses a one-bit sign, eight-bit biased exponent and 23-bit fraction. Decode 01000001011000000000000000000000 using bias 127 and the normal-number formula.

summary: A three-bit left shift produces 8n; adding n produces 9n.
steps: A left shift by k positions multiplies the represented integer by 2ᵏ when the mathematical result fits the available signed width.
Check the alternatives algebraically: (n<<2)+n = 5n; (n<<2)−n = 3n; (n<<3)+n = 9n; (n<<3)−n = 7n.
Only the third expression gives 9n, so choose C. Fixed-width overflow must be considered in an actual implementation.
takeaway: Translate each shift into a power of two before combining terms.

optionText.a: Shift left 2 bits, then add n.
optionText.b: Shift left 2 bits, then subtract n.
optionText.c: Shift left 3 bits, then add n.
optionText.d: Shift left 3 bits, then subtract n.

imageDescription: Choose a shift-and-add/subtract expression for 9 times a two’s-complement integer n.

summary: An AND mask retains the upper four bits and clears the lower four.
steps: For each bit x, x AND 1 = x, while x AND 0 = 0.
Apply mask 11110000. Its four high ones retain the corresponding source bits; its four low zeros force those result bits to zero.
NAND complements the desired AND result. OR with 00001111 sets the low bits to one, while XOR toggles them rather than clearing them. Choose A.
takeaway: Use AND with ones in positions to keep and zeros in positions to clear.
imageDescription: For an eight-bit integer, keep the most significant four bits in their original positions and make all other bits zero. Choose the appropriate bitwise operation.

summary: Push and pop use the stack pointer to locate the stack top.
steps: A stack stores items in last-in, first-out order. Push adds an item and pop removes the most recently added one.
The stack pointer tracks the stack position used by these operations; the exact increment/decrement convention depends on the architecture.
The instruction register holds an instruction, the program counter identifies an instruction address and the status register holds flags. None of those is the stack pointer. Choose C.
takeaway: Match each register to what it stores, rather than to a similar-sounding name.
imageDescription: Identify the special CPU register associated with push and pop instructions.

summary: The fetched instruction goes into the instruction register before decoding.
steps: Follow the arrows: main memory → a → instruction decoder. The value moving along this path is an instruction word.
The instruction register temporarily holds that fetched word so the decoder can interpret its opcode and operand fields.
The program counter stores an address; an accumulator stores arithmetic data; a data cache stores memory copies. Choose instruction register, option C.
takeaway: The PC points to an instruction; the IR contains the fetched instruction.
imageDescription: The diagram sends an instruction from main memory into a box marked a inside the processor, then into the instruction decoder. Identify box a.

summary: There are 16 million bus transfers per second, each carrying eight bytes.
steps: The 64 MHz input clock has 64×10⁶ cycles per second. One bus cycle takes four input cycles, so transfer frequency = 64×10⁶/4 = 16×10⁶ per second.
The 64-bit data bus carries 64/8 = 8 bytes per bus transfer.
The maximum rate is 16×10⁶×8 = 128×10⁶ bytes/s = 128 MB/s, option B. 512 MB/s would incorrectly assume one complete bus transfer per input clock.
takeaway: Divide by cycles per bus transfer and convert bits to bytes.
imageDescription: Calculate the theoretical rate of a 64-bit external bus driven by a 64 MHz clock when each bus cycle takes four input clock cycles.

summary: The main process receives the two milliseconds not occupied by handlers.
steps: The diagram has interrupt A at 1, 2.5 and 3.5 ms. Each high-priority A handler needs 0.5 ms: total A time is 1.5 ms.
B arrives at 0 ms and needs 1.5 ms. It runs from 0–1, is preempted by A from 1–1.5, and completes its remaining 0.5 ms from 1.5–2. The B arrival at 5 ms is outside the interval being measured.
The main process runs during 2–2.5, 3–3.5 and 4–5 ms: 0.5+0.5+1=2 ms, option A. Equivalently, 5−1.5−1.5=2.
takeaway: A preempted handler resumes its remaining work; it does not restart from the beginning.
imageDescription: Two nested interrupt priorities are permitted. A takes 0.5 ms and is higher priority; B takes 1.5 ms. A arrives at 1, 2.5 and 3.5 ms; B arrives at 0 and 5 ms. Find main-process CPU time in [0,5) ms, ignoring overhead.

summary: Both Q and R must be true.
steps: P is true, so NOT P is false. To make (NOT P) OR Q true, Q must be true.
With Q true, NOT Q is false. To make (NOT Q) OR R true, R must also be true.
The only compatible pair is Q=true and R=true, option D. Evaluate the first expression before using its consequence in the second.
takeaway: An OR expression with one false input can be true only if the other input is true.
imageDescription: P is true. Both (NOT P) OR Q and (NOT Q) OR R are true. Determine the truth values of Q and R.

summary: The multiplexer outputs X₂ when X₁=0, and NOT X₂ when X₁=1: XOR.
steps: The upper MUX input I₀ receives X₂ directly. The lower input I₁ receives NOT X₂. X₁ controls the select line.
For input pairs (X₁,X₂) = 00,01,10,11, the output is 0,1,1,0.
That is exactly XOR, the fourth gate symbol (D). AND outputs 1 only on 11; NAND is zero only on 11; OR is zero only on 00.
takeaway: Derive the MUX output separately for select 0 and select 1.
imageDescription: A 2-to-1 MUX selects I₀ for S=0 and I₁ for S=1. In the target circuit, I₀=X₂, I₁=NOT X₂ and S=X₁. Choices are AND, NAND, OR and XOR gate symbols.

summary: The circuit is a three-input NAND gate.
steps: The first gate produces NOT(x AND y). The separate z input has an inversion bubble before entering the final OR gate.
Therefore f = NOT(x AND y) OR NOT z. By De Morgan’s law this equals NOT(x AND y AND z).
Only option D is a three-input NAND. Its output is zero only for x=y=z=1. Option A lacks the output inversion; B and C combine different input groups.
takeaway: Treat an inversion bubble as NOT, then apply De Morgan’s law to the entire grouped expression.

optionText.a: Three-input AND: x AND y AND z
optionText.d: Three-input NAND: NOT(x AND y AND z)

imageDescription: x and y feed a NAND gate. Its output and inverted z feed an OR gate. Choose the equivalent circuit from the four diagrams described below.

summary: The output is NOT A AND B.
steps: The upper branch inverts A before NAND with B, giving U=NOT((NOT A) AND B)=A OR NOT B.
The lower branch is NOR(A,B), giving V=NOT(A OR B)=(NOT A) AND (NOT B). The final gate is NOR(U,V).
Absorption gives U OR V = A OR NOT B, so Y=NOT(A OR NOT B)=(NOT A) AND B. Choose B. Check: the output is 1 only when A=0 and B=1.
takeaway: Name intermediate gate outputs to avoid losing inversion bubbles.
imageDescription: In the diagram, the upper branch is NAND(NOT A,B), the lower branch is NOR(A,B), and both outputs enter a final NOR gate. Choose an equivalent Boolean expression.

summary: NAND is the negation of AND, so it is zero only when both inputs are one.
steps: AND is 1 only for A=B=1. Applying NOT reverses all four entries of that truth table.
NAND outputs 1,1,1,0 for inputs 00,01,10,11 respectively. This matches the required zero condition, option B.
OR is also zero on 00, and XOR is zero on both 00 and 11; those do not match “zero only when both inputs are one.”
takeaway: Read words such as only carefully: one matching row is not enough.
imageDescription: Choose a two-input, one-output circuit whose output is zero only when A and B are both one.

summary: The complete access takes approximately 27.92 ms.
steps: At 5,000 rpm, one rotation takes 60,000/5,000 = 12 ms. Average rotational latency is half of that: 6 ms.
Transfer time for 1 MB at 60 MB/s is 1/60 s = 16.6667 ms.

Add all specified components: 4 ms seek + 1.25 ms controller + 6 ms rotation + 16.6667 ms transfer = 27.9167 ms ≈ 27.92 ms, option C. Option D adds a full rotation instead of an average half-rotation.
takeaway: Use half a rotation for average rotational latency, and include every stated overhead.
imageDescription: An HDD has average seek 4 ms, controller overhead 1.25 ms, 5,000 rpm rotation and 60 MB/s transfer. Calculate average complete access time for 1 MB.

summary: With the stated binary unit convention, the complete access is 25.725 ms.
steps: One rotation at 6,000 rpm takes 60,000/6,000 = 10 ms, so average rotational latency is 5 ms.
The question explicitly defines 1 MB = 1,024 kB. Transfer time = 16/1,024 seconds = 0.015625 s = 15.625 ms.
Total = 5 ms seek + 0.1 ms controller + 5 ms rotation + 15.625 ms transfer = 25.725 ms, option B. Using a full rotation would give option C, 30.725 ms.
takeaway: Follow the problem’s unit definition instead of assuming that MB always uses the same convention.
imageDescription: An HDD has average seek 5 ms, 6,000 rpm rotation, 1 MB/s transfer and controller overhead 0.1 ms. Find complete average access time for 16 kB, using 1 MB = 1,024 kB.

summary: Defragmentation improves the placement of an HDD file’s blocks for access.
steps: A fragmented file occupies separated disk regions. Reading it can require extra head movement between fragments.
Defragmentation rearranges allocated blocks so related data is more contiguous, improving mechanical access efficiency: option A.
It is not junk-file deletion, does not remove physical interblock gaps, and cannot prevent a mechanical disk failure. The same mechanical-seek rationale does not apply to SSDs.
takeaway: Defragmentation changes block placement; it does not create a backup or repair hardware.

optionText.c: Delete interblock gaps to increase capacity

imageDescription: Choose the purpose of hard-disk defragmentation. Alternatives concern faster access, junk-file cleanup, removing interblock gaps, and preventing hardware failure.

summary: USB is the interface associated with a theoretical limit of 127 addressed devices.
steps: USB uses a host-controlled tiered arrangement, with hubs connecting multiple devices.
Its theoretical address space supports up to 127 addressed devices on a USB bus. Hubs consume addresses, and power, bandwidth and topology limits reduce practical expansion.
DisplayPort and HDMI primarily carry display/audio signals, and SATA connects storage devices. The quoted limit identifies USB, option D.
takeaway: A device-count limit is a logical addressing limit, not a promise of unlimited bandwidth or power.
imageDescription: Identify the interface that can theoretically connect up to 127 peripheral devices under PC control.

summary: A 3D printer fabricates a physical object from a digital model.
steps: Additive manufacturing creates an object layer by layer. Fused filament fabrication is one method: deposited thermoplastic forms successive layers.
That physical object-making function is option C. A 3D scanner performs the reverse direction, measuring an object to create digital shape data.
A hot head acting on heat-sensitive paper describes thermal printing; projecting images onto surfaces describes projection mapping. Neither fabricates the object.
takeaway: Distinguish physical fabrication, shape capture and image projection.

optionText.a: Measure a 3D object to produce digital shape data
optionText.b: Use a heated head on heat-sensitive paper
optionText.c: Fabricate an object using methods such as fused filament fabrication
optionText.d: Project computer graphics onto uneven objects

imageDescription: Choose the correct function of a 3D printer. This modern extension is linked to the chapter’s output-device discussion rather than assigned an invented 2015 textbook page.
